blocks.md: **The variance of US log hourly wages rose sharply in the 1980s (≈0.185 in 1979 to ≈0.23 in 1988), fell back to ≈0.20 around 2000 and rose again to ≈0.22 by 2009. Within-group variance is about two-thirds of the total. Holding the education mix fixed, the 2001 level equals 1979 and 2009 looks like the early 1970s.**
All values read off the lecture charts, approximate. Groups for the decomposition: 4 education × 2 gender × 2 race × 8 age = 128 cells, **not** composition-adjusted.
Between-cell share B/T ≈ 0.33 on average over the period.

- **The 1980s are exceptional**: the rise is pervasive — total, within and between all climb.
- **Post-1980s levels stay high, but much of that is composition**: the education mix shifted toward groups with higher within-group variance (see [US Within-Education Wage Variance 1973-2009](note:us-within-education-wage-variance-1973-2009)). Composition-adjusted, the gap between the post-2000 level and the 1970s mostly disappears — the adjustment fixes education shares as in [Composition Adjustment](note:composition-adjustment).
- **W depends on the cells**: with finer groups (more characteristics), more variance is labelled between and less within. "Two-thirds within" is for these 128 cells.

- **Data matter for dispersion**: May/MORG hourly wages are point-in-time measures; March-CPS hourly wages built from annual earnings, weeks and hours are noisier, and noise inflates the variance ([Classical Measurement Error](note:classical-measurement-error)). All CPS series are top-coded, so the variance is understated ([Top Coding](note:top-coding)).
- **Read the axis**: the same series replotted on a stretched vertical scale looks far more dramatic.
